messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun was thirty-four years old, a delivery driver for a regional courier company, and he had been behind the wheel for nearly a decade without incident. That changed on a rainy November afternoon when he was running behind schedule, trying to squeeze in one more drop before rush hour. He approached a poorly lit intersection, glanced at his dispatch screen for the next address, and felt a thud—heavy and final, nothing like the potholes he usually hit. He slammed the brakes and saw a man lying in the crosswalk, his bicycle crumpled a few feet away. Arjun jumped out, his hands shaking, and called 911, but by the time the ambulance arrived the man was unconscious with a head injury that later required emergency surgery. The police report said the victim would survive but would likely have permanent cognitive deficits. Arjun was not charged—the light was yellow, the victim had darted out—but he never stopped replaying the split second he looked away from the road.

In the weeks that followed, Arjun became convinced that he could have prevented the whole thing if he had been more alert, if he had left earlier, if he had honked, if he had braked a second sooner. He told himself over and over that he should have protected that man—it was his job as a driver to watch for pedestrians, and he had failed. The thought looped through his mind during every shift: *If I had just been paying attention, he would be fine.* He also carried a crushing sense of inaction guilt. He had gotten out of the truck, yes, but he felt he had not done enough. He had not known first aid; he had just stood there, frozen, while the man bled. He started to say to his wife, Meera, that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, for not somehow intervening before the collision. And the self-blame was specific: the event happened because of the way he acted—rushing, checking his phone, not pausing at the intersection. He began to see himself as reckless, careless, a danger to others.

Driving, once automatic, became a minefield. Every intersection made his palms sweat; every crosswalk he approached he slowed to a crawl, scanning for figures that might appear. He started taking longer routes to avoid three particular crossings near delivery zones—one where the accident had occurred, and two others that looked too similar. His manager noticed his delivery times slipping and warned him about efficiency. Arjun began dreading the start of his shift, but he could not afford to quit—the family needed his income, and Meera was pregnant with their first child. At home, he grew irritable and withdrawn. Meera would ask why he seemed so tired, and he would mutter about traffic, unable to tell her the truth because saying it aloud would make it real again. He stopped watching movies that showed car crashes, avoided news reports about traffic accidents, and found himself unable to drive past the hospital where the victim had been treated, even though it was not on his route.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment six months after the accident. He was driving home on a quiet residential street when he saw a child's soccer ball bounce into the road. He slammed the brakes so hard that the driver behind him nearly rear-ended him. The child ran out, grabbed the ball, and waved. Arjun sat in his truck, his heart hammering, and wept. He realized that his constant vigilance had not made him safer—it had made him terrified of every shadow. That night, he told Meera everything, and she encouraged him to see a therapist. Now he sits in the clinic, afraid that if he talks about it he will be swallowed by the guilt, but also quietly hoping that someone can help him trust his own hands on the wheel again.
